title: Mars has a canyon over 4,000 km long that reaches nearly a quarter of the way round

cover.alt: Mars seen as a full orange-red globe, with the dark gash of the Valles Marineris canyon system cutting across its middle from left to right.

body: Valles Marineris runs along the Martian equator for **more than 4,000 km**, up to 200 km wide, making it the largest canyon in the Solar System. Unlike Earth’s [Grand Canyon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Canyon), it was not carved by a river. The most widely agreed idea is that it is a vast crack in the crust, opened by rift faults as the crust thickened in the Tharsis volcanic region to its west, and later widened by erosion and collapsing walls. It is named after Mariner 9, the orbiter that discovered it in 1971–72.

slides.question: At its deepest, how many kilometres deep is Valles Marineris?
slides.explanation: Up to 7 km. The Grand Canyon in Arizona reaches about 1.9 km.

slides.heading: Canyon length, in kilometres
slides.note: Valles Marineris is more than 4,000 km long

left.label: Grand Canyon
left.text: 446 km long, up to 29 km wide and 1,857 m deep. Carved by the Colorado River.

right.label: Valles Marineris
right.text: Over 4,000 km long, 200 km wide and up to 7 km deep. Most likely a giant crack in the crust.

slides.alt: Orbital view of a deep canyon on Mars, with steep, rippled cliff walls dropping to a floor of landslide debris.
slides.caption: Ophir Chasma, one of the linked canyons of Valles Marineris, in a mosaic from the THEMIS camera on NASA’s Mars Odyssey orbiter.

Rift faults split the crust apart

slides.question: Why did 1970s scientists’ idea that water carved the canyon run into trouble?
options: Liquid water can’t last there today
Mars has no ice at all
slides.explanation: Liquid water cannot exist under most present-day Martian surface conditions, which makes water erosion a problematic explanation for a canyon this size.
